title: Old Blood Accelerated Alzheimer's in Mice, Reviving Debate Over Transfusion Risk
excerpt: Animal studies show Alzheimer's-linked proteins can travel through blood, but the largest human studies on whether transfusions raise dementia risk reach opposite conclusions.
body:
• Blood from aged mice accelerated beta-amyloid plaque buildup in Alzheimer's mouse models, while young blood showed protective effects, per a December 2025 study in the journal Aging.
  • A 2025 review identified multiple pathways — amyloid-beta seeding, tau protein, iron overload, inflammation, and herpesvirus — through which transfusions could theoretically influence Alzheimer's risk.
  • Large-scale human studies remain contradictory: a Scandinavian study of 1.47 million patients found no link, while a Taiwanese study of 127,000+ participants found a modest association.
  • There is no evidence Alzheimer's spreads through casual contact. Researchers stress that "transmissible does not equal contagious."

Blood From Old Mice Worsened Alzheimer's Pathology

Research published in the journal Aging in December 2025 found that weekly blood transfusions from old mice into Alzheimer's-prone Tg2576 transgenic mice accelerated the accumulation of amyloid plaques — the sticky protein clumps linked to the disease. Young blood, by contrast, appeared to slow the process.

The study, led by researchers at the Instituto Latinoamericano de Salud Cerebral (BrainLat) at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, alongside MELISA Institute, the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, and Universidad Mayor, involved 30 weeks of weekly blood infusions. Postmortem proteomic analysis of treated brains revealed more than 250 differentially expressed proteins linked to synaptic functions, endocannabinoid signaling, and calcium channels.

"By demonstrating that peripheral signals derived from aged blood can modulate central processes in the pathophysiology of Alzheimer's, these findings open new opportunities to study therapeutic targets aimed at the blood-brain axis."

— Dr. Claudia Durán-Aniotz, BrainLat, Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez

Can Alzheimer's Proteins Travel Through Blood?

The mouse study adds to a growing body of evidence that beta-amyloid (Aβ), the misfolded protein at the heart of Alzheimer's, behaves in prion-like fashion — capable of "seeding" healthy proteins into diseased forms.

A February 2025 narrative review published in Healthcare by researchers at the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College cataloged multiple pathways through which blood transfusions could raise Alzheimer's risk. Beyond direct Aβ transmission, the review identified iron overload from repeated transfusions, chronic inflammation triggered by blood components, and herpesvirus transmission as contributing mechanisms.

In animal models, the evidence is striking. A 2015 parabiosis experiment surgically joined Alzheimer's transgenic mice to healthy mice so they shared a circulatory system. After 12 months, the healthy mice developed vascular amyloid lesions, tau hyperphosphorylation, and neuroinflammation. A separate 2023 Chinese study found that injecting blood from Alzheimer's-model mice into healthy Kunming mice produced Aβ42 deposits in the hippocampus and measurable neuronal loss.

Human Studies Paint a Contradictory Picture

Whether any of this translates to humans remains an open question.

A landmark 2016 study led by Gustaf Edgren at Sweden's Karolinska Institutet tracked 1.47 million blood transfusion recipients over 44 years using Swedish-Danish databases. It found no association between receiving blood from donors who later developed neurodegenerative disease and the recipients' own Alzheimer's risk (hazard ratio: 0.99).

A 2019 Taiwanese study by Lin et al. reached a different conclusion. Analyzing 63,813 transfusion recipients and matched controls from the National Health Insurance Research Database, it found recipients had a modestly elevated risk of Alzheimer's (hazard ratio: 1.37). Patients who received washed red blood cells faced a higher risk still (hazard ratio: 2.37).

The studies used different definitions of exposure and controlled for different confounding variables, making direct comparison difficult. The Scandinavian study asked whether the donor later developed disease; the Taiwanese study examined the act of receiving a transfusion itself.

Contaminated Growth Hormone Provides a Cautionary Case

Some of the most concrete human evidence comes from an unexpected source. In 2024, researchers reported five individuals who received cadaveric-derived human growth hormone contaminated with Aβ seeds during childhood and developed early-onset dementia meeting Alzheimer's diagnostic criteria — more than 30 years after exposure.

Biochemical analysis confirmed the injected hormone contained both Aβ and tau proteins. When residual material from original vials — stored at room temperature for over three decades — was injected into the brains of transgenic mice, it produced amyloid deposits and cerebral amyloid angiopathy. The proteins had remained transmissible after 30-plus years of storage.

"It is important — imperative — to emphasize that transmissible does not equal contagious. There is absolutely no evidence that people with dementia can spread their disease casually to people around them."

— Scientific American

What It Means for Public Safety

The World Health Organization already permanently defers blood donation for people with dementia, neurodegenerative diseases, or a history of receiving pituitary-derived growth hormone. The Healthcare review's authors proposed that if further research confirms a transfusion link, screening donors with plasma p-tau217 biomarkers — now recognized as accurate early indicators of preclinical Alzheimer's — could serve as a practical safeguard.

No blood bank currently screens for Alzheimer's-related proteins, and the evidence does not yet justify changing transfusion practices. But researchers across multiple institutions agree: the question warrants larger, longer prospective studies using modern biomarker tools — particularly as the global population ages and demand for transfusions rises.
